cues.text: The Fisherman of Galilee
Simon was a fisherman of Bethsaida on the Sea of Galilee, the son of Jona and brother of the Apostle Andrew , who first brought him to Jesus.
At that meeting the Lord looked on him and said he would be called Cephas — Aramaic for rock — rendered in Greek as Petros .
It was an unusual promise to make to a rough, impulsive fisherman, and the Gospels never hide his faults: he sinks in the water for lack of faith, he misunderstands, he presumes.
Yet from the beginning Christ singled him out, and Simon left his nets to follow.
Prince of the Apostles
At Caesarea Philippi, when Jesus asked who the disciples believed him to be, it was Peter who answered for them all.

To that confession the Lord replied with the words on which the Roman primacy has ever since been founded: that upon this rock he would build his Church, and that the gates of hell would not prevail against it.
He also gave Peter the keys of the kingdom of heaven.

Across the Gospels Peter stands consistently first: first in every list of the Apostles, spokesman for the Twelve, the one who walks briefly on the water and who is present at the Transfiguration and in Gethsemane.
He is, in the ancient title, the Prince of the Apostles.
Denial and Restoration
His confidence outran his strength.

At the Last Supper he swore he would die rather than deny his Master; hours later, in the courtyard of the high priest, he denied three times that he even knew him, and wept bitterly when the cock crowed.
It is the measure of the Gospel's honesty that this failure is recorded of the very man given the keys.
The risen Christ healed the wound with deliberate symmetry.
By the Sea of Tiberias he asked Peter three times whether he loved him, and three times entrusted him with his flock: Feed my lambs; feed my sheep.
The threefold denial was answered by a threefold commission to shepherd the whole Church.
Leader of the Infant Church
After the Ascension Peter takes charge at once.

He proposes the choice of a successor to Judas; he preaches at Pentecost , and three thousand are baptized; he works the first miracle of healing and gives the first defence of the faith before the Sanhedrin.
It is to Peter that God reveals, in the vision at Joppa and the baptism of the centurion Cornelius, that the Gentiles are to be admitted to the Church without first becoming Jews.
At the Council of Jerusalem his testimony is central to the discussion, while James gives the judgment accepted by the assembled Apostles and elders.
The Two Epistles
Two letters of the New Testament bear Peter's name.

The First Epistle of Peter , written from Rome — which he calls, in the veiled language of the persecuted Church, Babylon — encourages Christians scattered through Asia Minor to stand firm under suffering.
It reminds them that they are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation.
The Second Epistle warns against false teachers and against the mockers who doubt that the Lord will return.
Together they show the fisherman become a father to the churches, writing with the plain authority of one who had walked with Christ and seen his glory on the holy mountain.
Rome and Martyrdom
Ancient and unbroken tradition brings Peter at last to Rome , where he governed the Church and, with St. Paul , gave the city its two great Apostles.
During the persecution that followed the fire of Rome under Nero , about the year 64–67, he was put to death.
By a tradition recorded from early times he asked to be crucified head downward, counting himself unworthy to die in the same posture as his Lord.
He was buried nearby on the Vatican Hill.

Excavations under St. Peter's Basilica in the twentieth century uncovered a first-century grave and monument venerated as his from the earliest period, and in 1968 the relics found there were declared to be, in all probability, the Apostle's own.
The Rock of the Church
Peter's successors in the see of Rome are the popes, who exercise to this day the office of confirming the brethren that Christ committed to him.
His feast, kept with St. Paul on June 29 , is among the oldest in the Roman calendar.
In Christian art he is shown with the keys of heaven, often with an inverted cross, a boat, or a rooster recalling his denial — the fisherman who became, in the Lord's own phrase, a fisher of men.
